# Appendix: Resources

> "Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit."
>
> — Psalm 34:18

## If you are in crisis {-}

This comes first, ahead of the book list, because it matters most.

Are you thinking about ending your life or harming yourself? Is the darkness you're in deeper than a bad week? Then please stop reading and get help now.

- **If you're in immediate danger, call your local emergency number.**
- **Contact a suicide or crisis helpline in your country.** In the United States you can call or text 988. Elsewhere, search for "crisis helpline" with the name of your country, or ask a doctor.
- **Talk to someone today.** It could be a friend, a family member, a pastor or a doctor. Do it today, and say the true thing out loud to a human being.

What you're feeling is not the Little Monster, and it isn't a verdict on you. This habit loads a man with shame, and shame lies about how things will turn out. You're worth more than the worst thing you've done. No book can do the job of a person, though, so please go and find one.

## If it began with something done to you {-}

Chapter 28 said that for some men this habit started after they were abused as children, and that most of them have never told anyone. If that's you, this section is yours.

What was done to you was not your sin, and it wasn't your fault. The habit that grew up afterwards is the kind this book can help with. The wound under it needs a person.

- **Tell one safe person.** A counsellor trained in trauma is the best choice. Ask for exactly that, in those words: "trauma-informed". A good doctor can refer you.
- **Use a sexual-abuse helpline.** They are free and confidential, and nobody there will be shocked. In the United States, RAINN runs one on 1-800-656-4673 and at rainn.org. Elsewhere, search for "sexual abuse helpline" with the name of your country.
- **If the person who hurt you was in the church,** you may not want to begin with a pastor. Begin with a counsellor or a helpline. God isn't offended.

You don't have to tell the whole story on the first day. Saying one sentence to one person is enough to begin.

## Getting ordinary help {-}

Most readers will never need more than this book and a friend. If you do, there's no shame in it.

- **Your pastor or an elder.** Chapter 28 covered how to tell him, and Chapter 30 told him how to listen.
- **A Christian counsellor.** See one if the habit is tangled up with something older and heavier, such as grief, abuse or a marriage in trouble. If you're not a believer, any good counsellor who takes the problem seriously will do.
- **Your doctor.** See a doctor about sleep that doesn't mend, low mood that doesn't lift, and anything about your body that worries you. This book has stayed out of medicine from the first page. A doctor is the person to ask.
- **One honest friend.** He's the cheapest help on this list and often the best.
- **For wives.** You need someone of your own to talk to, as Chapter 30 said. That might be a wise older woman, a pastor or a counsellor.

Apart from the two helplines above, I haven't listed organisations, clinics or programmes by name. I don't know your country or your church, and I'd rather give you no address than a wrong one.

## Further reading {-}

Everything below was drawn on in writing this book. I've said honestly where an item and this book disagree.

### The books this one grew from {-}

- **[*EasyPeasy*](https://easypeasymethod.org/)** by Hackauthor². It's free, and it's the free online book this one is modelled on, chapter for chapter. This book grew out of it. Read it too.
- **Allen Carr, *The Easy Way to Stop Smoking*.** The method comes from here. It's worth reading even if you've never smoked, just to watch the method work on a different trap.

### Old books that have lasted {-}

- **Augustine, *Confessions*, Book 8.** He prays "not yet", hears a child's voice in a garden, and is free the same day. It was written sixteen centuries ago and it's the best account of a divided will that I know. E.B. Pusey's translation is in the public domain and [free to read online](https://faculty.georgetown.edu/jod/augustine/Pusey/book08).
- **John Owen, *The Mortification of Sin* (1656).** The classic on putting sin to death. Owen sounds like the opposite of this book, since he calls the fight a daily work. But he insists it can only be done by the Spirit and never by grit, so he's really on our side. The prose is hard going and worth the effort.
- **Thomas Chalmers, "The Expulsive Power of a New Affection".** It's a single sermon, and it explains better than anything else why a desire leaves only when a greater love arrives. It's [free online](https://www.preceptaustin.org/expulsive-power-of-a-new-affection).

### C.S. Lewis {-}

- ***Mere Christianity*, Book III, chapter 5, "Sexual Morality".** It's short and sane, and there's no panic in it.
- ***The Screwtape Letters*.** A senior devil explains temptation to a junior one. You'll recognise the Big Monster's whole method, including pleasures that shrink while the demand for them grows.
- ***The Four Loves*, the chapter on Eros.** It's about the difference between wanting a sensation and loving a person.
- **His 1956 letter to Keith Masson**, printed in the third volume of his *Collected Letters*. This is where the "harem of imaginary brides" comes from. I've only seen the parts that others quote, and those alone are worth a library trip.

### More recent Christian writing {-}

- **Dietrich Bonhoeffer, *Temptation*.** A brief book about how suddenly desire wakes, and whose strength a man stands in when it does.
- **John Piper, ["Missions and Masturbation"](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/missions-and-masturbation)** and ["Strategies for Fighting Sexual Sin"](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/strategies-for-fighting-sexual-sin). Piper is a fighter, and his language is all battle. Read him for his seriousness and his hope. Don't let the battle language talk you back into the Willpower Method.
- **Heath Lambert, *Finally Free*.** It's written about pornography, and grace is its subject from start to finish. It applies to the hand as well.
- **Tim Challies, ["Self-Centered Sex"](https://www.challies.com/articles/self-centered-sex-part-2/).** A plain-spoken pastor on why the habit isolates a man.
- **Brittany Allen, ["Debunking 4 Justifications for Masturbation"](https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/debunking-justifications-masturbation/)**. A careful answer to "but is it really a sin?"
- **Johnathan Arnold, ["Is Masturbation a Sin?"](https://holyjoys.org/is-masturbation-sin/)**. He says to stop at once and completely, and we agree.
- **Luke Gilkerson, ["Three Steps to Kick the Habit of Masturbation"](https://www.covenanteyes.com/blog/three-steps-to-kick-the-habit-of-masturbation/).** His advice to find the lies you believe and replace them with truth is this book in miniature. Under the article are years of readers' comments, and many of the testimonies quoted here came from them. One difference: the site that hosts it sells accountability software, and this book doesn't ask you to use any.
- **Craig Groeschel, ["When the Urge Is Too Strong"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xzzJ6uLnbQ)** (a sermon). The M&Ms in Chapter 25 and the "was it worth it?" story in Chapter 14 are his. He is funny, and honest about himself.
- **Mike Novotny, ["What Does God and the Bible Say About Masturbation?"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hcra9n8aMyg)** (a talk). A pastor who admits straight away that the Bible never names the habit, and then shows why that doesn't settle it.
- **Ezekiel ("Brother Zeke"), ["How Mast\*rbation Had Me Bound but God"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mppw_mrhlIY)** (a testimony). Caught at ten, free as a man. Several of the best lines in this book are his, or come from the comments under his video. His tradition speaks more about spirits than this book does.
- **Jason Evert, ["Freedom from Lust"](https://bustedhalo.com/podcasts/jason-evert-on-freedom-from-lust/)** (a podcast interview). A Catholic speaker on chastity as the thing that makes love possible.

### Voices from outside the church {-}

- **FitXFearless** (Bismarck Ebiweh) on YouTube. He's blunt and energetic, and he's honest about what the habit costs a young man. We've quoted him gratefully. We don't follow him when he sells quitting as a way to attract women, or when he describes semen as a man's energy source. Take what's honest from him and leave those two.
- **Other coaches and channels.** Captain Sinbad, QuitByHealing and Nick Jones on YouTube were all drawn on. QuitByHealing's advice on urges, to notice them and do nothing, is the nearest thing to this book's method that I found outside EasyPeasy. Captain Sinbad describes the first weeks well, but he recommends turning lust into ambition, and this book doesn't.
- **Dr Doug Weiss, ["The Real Way to Quit Masturbating for Good"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vmlk6YdWLuY).** A Christian therapist with decades of clients behind him. He is good on secrecy and on abuse. He recommends rewards and punishments, and Chapter 19 explains why we don't.
- **The NoFap forum.** Many of the men quoted in this book wrote there. See the caution below.
- **Phineas 808, ["16 Principles of Recovery"](https://www.yourbrainonporn.com/tools-for-change-recovery-from-porn-addiction/rebooting-advice-observations-from-successful-rebooters/16-principles-of-recovery/).** A short list by a man who got out. His line about becoming "a man who does not" is as close to this book's method as anything on the forums.
- **Maxwell Maltz, *Psycho-Cybernetics*.** The ringing telephone in Chapter 27 is his.
- **James Clear, *Atomic Habits*,** and **Wendy Wood, *Good Habits, Bad Habits*.** Two plain accounts of how habits hang on cues, if you'd like the everyday mechanics.
- **Cleveland Clinic, ["Are 'Wet Dreams' Normal and Healthy?"](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/wet-dreams)** For the reader who's still worried after Chapter 28.

A caution about forums in general. You'll find real honesty there, and you'll also find day counters, miracle claims and men on their fortieth reset. Read the testimonies if they help you. Leave the counters where they are.

## Coping lines {-}

EasyPeasy's appendix has a list of statements for hard moments, taken from a school of counselling that teaches people to answer their own bad thinking. Here is our version. These lines aren't spells. Each one is a true sentence to set against a false one. Read through them once, mark the two or three that fit you, and keep those.

1. "A feeling is not an order. I can feel this and do nothing about it, and it'll go."
2. "This urge is the leftover of a habit, and that's all it is. It tells me nothing about what I need."
3. "It never fixed a bad day. I got the same bad day back with shame added."
4. "I'm uncomfortable. I'm not in danger. No man ever died of an evening."
5. "I'd like to feel better this minute. Wanting that doesn't give me a reason to do something that makes me feel worse."
6. "My wife, my boss and the weather don't have to behave well for me to stay free. My freedom doesn't hang on any of them."
7. "I failed before. That's a fact about some days in my past, and it's no forecast."
8. "If I fall, I've fallen. I haven't become a failure. I confess it, I get up, and I look for the instruction I broke."
9. "I don't have to be impressive today. I only have to be honest."
10. "Loneliness hurts, and it's telling me to go and find people. It isn't telling me to shut the door."
11. "Boredom is not an emergency."
12. "I'm tired. Tired men believe lies more easily. I'll go to bed, with the phone in the other room."
13. "I am forgiven. I don't have to earn it by being miserable."
14. "The thought came, and I didn't invite it. Thinking it doesn't make it true, and I won't obey it."
15. "YES! I'M FREE!"

If you're a Christian, turn any of them into a prayer by putting "Lord" at the front and meaning it. Then go back to the verses in Chapter 31.

## Whose voice is that? {-}

EasyPeasy's appendix ends with an essay by one of its readers. He joins the method to a technique of Jack Trimpey's for recognising what Trimpey calls the addictive voice. The essay is addressed to the small number of men who've seen through every lie in the book and are still getting tripped up. I've retold its main point here in this book's terms, because it's useful and the credit should go where it's due.

The point is this. **The old lie speaks in your voice and says "I".**

The Little Monster is only an itch, and an itch can't talk. The voice belongs to the Big Monster, the lies, speaking up for the itch. He doesn't announce himself. He never says, "This is your old habit speaking." He says, "I could do with it tonight." "I've had a rough week." "I deserve something." It sounds exactly like your own thinking, so you take it for your own.

There's a simple test. Say No, plainly, and listen to what comes back. The grammar changes. "I could do with it" becomes "Oh, come on, *you* know you want to." "I deserve it" becomes "After all *we've* been through?" Something that has to switch to "you" and "we" in order to keep arguing with you isn't you. You've caught him.

Here's a second test. Hold up your hand and wiggle your fingers. Now ask the urge to do it. He can't. He has no hands of his own, and he's never once done the deed himself. He can only talk until you lend him yours. You're the one in the driving seat, and you always were.

Two things follow.

**The feelings are his as well.** When you say No, you may get a pang of sadness. You may get a flicker of fear that something precious is being taken away. That pang isn't your heart speaking. It's his tantrum. Once you can see whose feeling it is, it loses its grip, and you may even find it funny.

**Hearing the voice doesn't mean you believe the lies again.** This is why the essay matters. A man hears "I want it" in his own head and panics: "I thought I'd seen through all that. The book hasn't worked. I must still believe the lies." So he starts the book again, and then again, hunting for a lie that isn't there. Ask yourself one question: *do I actually believe what that voice just said?* If the honest answer is no, your understanding is fine. You've only heard a noise. Let it ring, as Chapter 27 said, and be glad you can tell the difference.

Paul described the same thing in a single line. Looking at the pull he felt in his own body, he wrote, "So now it is no more I that do it, but sin which dwells in me." He wasn't making an excuse. He was telling the two voices apart. One of them is you, and the other is a squatter who was served notice the day you prayed.

When he speaks up, you needn't argue or get angry. Recognise him, smile, and say what you always say.

**"YES! I'M FREE!"**
